item.title: Museums help build bridges for civilizations
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-07
Museums help build bridges for civilizations Appreciating past, present and future aids mutual learning, dialogue and inclusiveness A decade after President Xi Jinping and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi toured Luxor, a city widely known as one of the world's largest open-air museums, the two leaders again stepped into the world of ancient Egypt — this time at the Grand Egyptian Museum on the Giza Plateau. On Wednesday, during Xi's state visit to Egypt, the two presidents and their wives visited the museum, viewing treasures including the throne, golden mask and royal chariots of Tutankhamun. Surrounded by artifacts tracing thousands of years of Egyptian civilization, Xi called the museum "a book with endless pages". During the tour, Xi noted that China and Egypt are both ancient civilizations and countries rich in World Heritage sites. He called on the two sides to uphold a vision of civilization based on equality, mutual learning, dialogue and inclusiveness, implement the Global Civilization Initiative, and promote inclusive coexistence and mutual learning among different civilizations. Museums have been repeatedly featured in Xi's engagement with history and civilization — as places for understanding cultural roots and as settings for encounters with other civilizations. In a congratulatory letter to the first UNESCO High-Level Forum on Museums in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, in November 2016, Xi described museums as important places for protecting and passing on human civilizations and as bridges linking the past, present and future, with a special role in exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations. Whether on domestic inspection tours or overseas trips, Xi's visits have taken him to many museums, such as the Sanxingdui Museum in Sichuan province and the Yinxu Museum in Henan province, key sites of early Chinese civilization. During a visit in April 2021 to the Anthropology Museum of Guangxi in Nanning, the capital of the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, Xi said that he made time to visit museums during local inspection tours to better understand a place's historical and cultural development. At a symposium at the Dunhuang Academy in Gansu province in August 2019, Xi spoke about cultural confidence and learning from other civilizations. "Only a self-confident civilization can absorb and draw on the achievements of other civilizations while maintaining its own characteristics," he said, calling for broader cultural exchanges with other countries and more active efforts to learn from the achievements of civilizations around the world. Dong Biao, a researcher at Peking University's Institute of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, said museums preserve both the tangible achievements and the cultural and intellectual legacy of human civilizations, enabling people to engage more directly with the creativity, ways of life and ideas of past societies. A deeper understanding of one's own history and culture can strengthen cultural identity and confidence, Dong said. For Xi, museums offer people a chance to discover unfamiliar histories, recognize common threads of human creativity and gain a deeper understanding of one another. "In the many places I have visited around the world, what fascinates me the most is civilizations in their rich diversity," Xi said at the opening of the Conference on Dialogue of Asian Civilizations in May 2019. Xi's overseas visits over the years have included stops at museums and historic sites such as the Amir Timur Museum in Uzbekistan and the ancient Maya ruins of Chichen Itza in Mexico. At the Acropolis Museum in Athens, Greece, in November 2019, one such cultural encounter unfolded around a single artifact. Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, were visiting the museum with then Greek president Prokopis Pavlopoulos and his wife when they stopped before the relief known as the "Pensive Athena". Pavlopoulos explained that Athena, the goddess of warfare and wisdom in Greek mythology, was resting and contemplating after battle. Xi said she was reflecting on what war meant and cited the ancient Chinese idiom "zhi ge wei wu", which means that to be able to stop war is the true art of war. Xi later said the museum visit had deepened his understanding of ancient Greek civilization and made him further realize how much the Chinese and Greek civilizations have in common. Museums have also served as settings in which Xi introduced China's history and cultural ideas to visiting foreign leaders. During Donald Trump's first state visit to China in November 2017, Xi and Peng accompanied the US president and first lady Melania Trump through the Palace Museum, or Forbidden City. As they walked along its central axis, Xi introduced the history, architecture and culture of the ancient palace. They visited the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the Hall of Central Harmony and the Hall of Preserving Harmony, whose names reflect the Chinese cultural ideal of harmony. Wang Yiwei, vice-president of the Academy of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era at Renmin University of China, said that exchanges among civilizations are not only about preserving the past, but also about how societies understand one another in the present. He said the Global Civilization Initiative put forward by Xi reflects this emphasis by calling for respect for the diversity of civilizations and for equality, mutual learning, dialogue and inclusiveness. At a time of geopolitical rivalry, conflicts and differences over values, Wang said that dialogue among civilizations cannot replace political negotiations or resolve disagreements over national interests. But it can help countries better understand one another's histories, identities and development paths, reduce misperceptions and strengthen the basis for mutual understanding. zhaojia@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Cooking a peaceful plotline
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-07
For most foreigners learning Chinese, nihao (hello) and xiexie (thank you) are the most common first words. Omar Sherif, however, found himself saying a different Chinese phrase far more frequently: shou gong — "it's a wrap". The 16-year-old Egyptian actor has won over Chinese audiences this summer with Once Upon a Time in the Middle East, which topped the country's daily box office for 25 consecutive days following its release on Aug 11. In the movie, Sherif — who was cast when he was 13 — plays Seif, a local orphan in an unnamed war-torn Middle Eastern country. Gifted with a talent for cooking, the boy is taken in as an apprentice by Xu Fu, a veteran Chinese chef played by Shen Teng. Xu is a debt-ridden father who leaves home to work at a Middle Eastern restaurant and chooses to stay and earn more money after the country is suddenly plunged into war. In the early days, life remains relatively peaceful. His boss, a local official, manages to keep the restaurant supplied with electricity and water despite the conflict. With his excellent culinary skills, Xu turns the restaurant into not only a local favorite but also a gathering place for soldiers, journalists and embassy employees. Alongside his friend Ma Junsheng, the restaurant's front-desk manager played by Jiang Qiming, Xu takes in more than 20 orphans, including Seif. But the seemingly peaceful days do not last. Xu and Ma, along with Seif, are wrongly imprisoned after being suspected of their involvement in a bombing. Just days before their scheduled release, they fall into the hands of a group of extremist militants. Seif loses an eye while trying to protect the two men. When Xu discovers that the extremists plan to train orphans as suicide bombers, he risks his life to lead the children on a desperate escape — but the story takes an even more complicated turn. For Sherif, the role was more than a demanding acting experience. Selected from more than 6,000 young hopefuls in Egypt, he tells China Daily that working on a Chinese film was an entirely new experience. With Chinese ancestry — his great-grandfather was from Shandong province — Sherif spent three months in Egypt learning Mandarin and Chinese cooking techniques before joining the production.

item.title: Rescue teams intensify deep searches in Gyirong
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-07
Rescue teams intensify deep searches in Gyirong Forty-three people are confirmed dead and 519 remain missing in Gyirong county, Xizang autonomous region, after a devastating mudslide swept through the area on Aug 26, as search and rescue operations continued, local authorities said on Sunday. Ren Wei, commander of the frontline headquarters and executive vice-chairman of the regional government, said during a news conference in Gyirong that, as of 6 pm on Saturday, 993 items of personal belongings recovered. As of Saturday evening, more than 2,500 rescuers had been deployed, along with over 500 vehicles and more than 9,000 sets of rescue equipment. Drones had made over 1,000 flights, while 5.43 metric tons of supplies and equipment had been air-dropped. Since road access to the core area was restored on Wednesday, six specialized groups and seven rescue teams have been carrying out detailed searches. Rescuers have been clearing debris layer by layer and searching each section thoroughly, with some areas already cleared down to the original foundations. Ren said searches will continue under the existing plan to ensure the core disaster area is covered as thoroughly as possible. Meanwhile, authorities are providing support to the families of the dead and missing. A dedicated hotline has taken 675 calls from relatives so far, while 791 family members had been received and 640 of them accommodated. Two local villagers had been rescued late last month. Pu Weidong, executive deputy head of the regional public security department, said more than 60 forensic specialists and three laboratories had been mobilized to identify the victims. Remains and personal belongings are being registered and documented, while fingerprints, genetic information and other identifying features are being collected and cross-checked with information provided by relatives. Pu said the work is being carried out scientifically, rigorously and carefully, with full respect for the dignity of the deceased and local customs. Pu added that the authorities would regularly release information about the search, rescue and follow-up work. A 24-hour hotline has also been established to respond to families' concerns, with further updates to be released according to developments in the search and identification process. Preventing secondary disasters remains the priority. More than 100 experts and technical personnel have been deployed, along with 150 sets of professional monitoring equipment to track slope deformation, water levels, weather conditions and other factors. Deng Buchuan, deputy director of the special disaster rescue department of Xizang Fire and Rescue, said the team is searching through the mud layer by layer. "I hope more people can be rescued and we will do as much as we can to the best of our ability," he said. Su Pengcheng, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, said experts have monitored barrier lakes, unstable slopes, glaciers and glacial lakes, while surveying geological hazards around five villages and along the emergency route. He said a high-altitude ice-rock collapse on the Nepalese side of the Himalayas triggered the disaster. The resulting debris flow traveled about 22 kilometers downstream in only six to seven minutes, causing severe damage. Although a barrier lake that had formed after the disaster has drained naturally, Su said unstable deposits and slopes remain, creating risks of localized blockages, landslides and debris. Satellite and aerial remote sensing, radar, hydrological monitoring and real-time drone imagery are being used to support continuous risk assessment and provide warnings to rescuers downstream. Su said climate change is increasing the risks of disasters in the Himalayas, calling for early glacier-risk assessment, an integrated satellite, aerial and ground monitoring system and stronger cross-border cooperation on data sharing, risk assessment and early warning. Foreign journalists visiting the site also noted the difficulty of reaching the remote area. Muhammad Asghar, a correspondent for the Associated Press of Pakistan in China, said the rescue response had been "very quick" despite the challenging access. Bruno Falci, a Brazilian journalist with Latin American television channel teleSUR, said it was "really impressive how fast China acts", citing the rapid mobilization of rescuers and reopening of roads. The State Council Information Office and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs organized a visit to the disaster area on Saturday and Sunday for 17 journalists from nine overseas media outlets, including those from the United States, Britain, Russia, India and Singapore. Contact the writers at yangzekun@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Rail link boosts red tourism
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-07
Rail link boosts red tourism High-speed train to connect former revolutionary bases, foster ties Ruijin and Yan'an, two cities central to China's revolutionary history, gained their first direct high-speed train service on Sunday, opening new opportunities for tourism and exchanges between the former revolutionary bases. The G3998 Fuxing train departed Ruijin in Jiangxi province at 11:02 am for Yan'an in Shaanxi province. The 1,857-kilometer journey will take about 11 hours and pass through Jiangxi, Hubei and Shaanxi provinces. Services in both directions will begin on Monday. The new service comes as China marks the 90th anniversary of the completion of the Long March, the Communist Party of China's strategic retreat between 1934 and 1936 that brought the CPC to northern Shaanxi. Ruijin was an early revolutionary base and one of the places where the Red Army began the Long March, while Yan'an served as the base of the CPC leadership from 1937 to 1947. The direct service is expected to boost "red tourism" — visits to sites associated with China's revolutionary history — by allowing travelers to visit both cities without changing trains. "This summer, we saw a noticeable increase in passengers visiting former revolutionary bases," said Feng Chenhu, a train conductor based in Xi'an, Shaanxi. "Trips to revolutionary sites across different regions have become particularly popular." For tourism operators, the direct service provides opportunities to develop travel routes that previously required more complex arrangements. Liu Wei, who oversees the Hongjing revolutionary site in Ruijin, said the service would make it easier to organize educational tours linking southern Jiangxi and northern Shaanxi, helping the two regions attract visitors interested in their shared revolutionary history. A Yan'an culture and tourism official said the city was already working with tourism authorities in Ruijin and nearby Yudu, inviting travel agencies to visit Yan'an and jointly promote Long March-themed itineraries. Both Ruijin and Yudu have introduced incentives to encourage rail passengers to spend more time and money locally. Travelers who present train tickets to the respective destinations can receive benefits, including free admission to participating attractions and discounts on performances, hotels and local specialties. The service will become a vital cog in the successive additions to China's high-speed rail network. The Xi'an-Yan'an line opened in December, bringing Yan'an onto the high-speed rail network, while the Xi'an-Shiyan railway opened on June 30, strengthening links between Shaanxi and Hubei. Together with existing lines in Jiangxi, these connections enabled the new service. Beyond tourism, the train is also intended to serve people visiting relatives, traveling for work and conducting business, said Yang Liang, an engineer in the passenger transport department of China Railway Nanchang Group. The northbound service will be accessible to 27 stations along the route, including Nanchang and Wuhan, extending its reach beyond the two terminal cities. Stations along the route are preparing to guide passengers and provide information about local revolutionary history. For Liu Yutong, a Yan'an native who works at the city's railway station, the new connection also offers a chance to share the city's story with a wider audience. A member of the station's foreign-language service team, Liu provides assistance to Chinese and international visitors interested in the city's revolutionary past. "As someone who works at Yan'an station, I look forward to welcoming visitors from far away and telling them how this place has changed," she said. luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: 43 dead, 519 missing after mudslide hits border port in Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-07
President Xi Jinping urges all-out rescue, relief efforts after mudslide hits border port in Xizang Level-II emergency response activated after mudslide hits border port in Xizang China on Monday said it had invited foreign journalists to visit the mudslide-hit areas of Gyirong in the Xizang autonomous region to learn about rescue efforts and reconstruction progress in response to the international media's close attention to reporting on the debris flow disaster. The visit came after round-the-clock repair work had initially reopened the roads to the disaster zone, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said at a regular news briefing. China had invited journalists from eight foreign media outlets, including NBC, CNN, Reuters, RT and the Press Trust of India, to enter the hardest-hit areas to learn about rescue and reconstruction progress, Mao said. They also attended a news conference held by the regional government, she added. As reports from these journalists have been released, Mao said, "China will continue to make every effort to carry out search-and-rescue operations and handling of the aftermath, and release the latest information on the disaster and rescue operations in a timely manner." After days of relentless search and rescue efforts, Xiao Fugui, a police officer at the entry-exit border inspection station in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, looked gaunt and exhausted. Despite his weary appearance, he repeatedly insisted that he was not at all tired. "All I want is to find my workmates," he said on Thursday, gripping an iron shovel with determination, his brow furrowed. On Aug 26, a massive mudslide devastated Gyirong Port, a vital land link between China and Nepal. As of 6 pm on Saturday, 993 personal belongings had been recovered while 519 people remain unaccounted for. Xiao was driving toward the port when the disaster struck. "I was just 4 or 5 kilometers away when I saw several cars pulled over," he said. "I got out and asked other drivers what was happening — everyone was panicked, saying the water level had risen sharply near the port." Concerned for their safety, he instructed the two female colleagues in his car to get out and find a safe place, then continued driving alone to assess the situation. Upon realizing it was a mudslide, Xiao immediately alerted authorities. "The muddy water was rushing toward me, so I threw the car into reverse and backed up about 500 meters before stopping," said Xiao in a tense voice. "I was terrified the car would be swept away. What really scared me was not knowing what had happened to my workmates at the port." As visibility dropped sharply and the road ahead was blocked, Xiao found himself trapped. Reflecting on that moment, he said, "I really walked through the gates of hell that day." Driven by worry and a deep sense of duty, Xiao joined the rescue teams. By Sunday, he had reached the vicinity of the port and immediately immersed himself in the relief efforts. "As soon as I arrived, I started moving supplies, then began searching. I found clothing, shoes and crushed vehicles belonging to the missing. Every single item I saw pierced my heart like a needle." Originally from Qinghai province, 39-year-old Xiao has worked in Xizang for 17 years, with 11 of those years at the Gyirong entry-exit border inspection station, primarily handling publicity affairs. "For many years, I've spent almost every day with my workmates — filming their patrols, writing about their lives guarding this border," he said. "This port, these people — they've become part of me." On the first day of the rescue, Xiao and other workers camped in a tent by a reservoir halfway up the mountain near the border port. He did not sleep at all. "The rain was so heavy that night — water poured down the slopes and merged into the river. The sound of rain, rushing water and collapsing hillsides all mixed together. It made my heart sink. I didn't dare to sleep, and I couldn't sleep anyway," he said. As he spoke, he picked up the shovel and resumed digging. "I have only one thought: no matter what, I want to find my workmates. I want to bring them home," he added. Contact the writers at caoyin@chinadaily.com.cn As dawn broke in Gyirong county following another night of continuous rain on Saturday, He Lei, a psychological counselor, began another day of providing counseling services to search and rescue personnel working on the front line of the mudslide-stricken Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region. "Through our work these days, we have found that our soldiers are quite resilient. They are focused on fulfilling their missions here and are fully aware of the significance of helping every family affected by the disaster," said He, a member of the medical and disease prevention team with the logistics support department of the People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command. As of Thursday, the PLA and the People's Armed Police Force had deployed 726 personnel to support rescue and relief operations following the mudslide, according to official data. Li Guokai, head of the medical and disease prevention team, said the team is responsible for providing medical and psychological services to rescue workers and affected villagers during patrol visits, disinfecting key sites and monitoring health risks. According to He, for those experiencing stress responses such as panic attacks or physical stiffness, the most important thing is to divert their attention from whatever is triggering the reaction. "We have a method called 'look, listen, smell and move.' For instance, we will guide soldiers in need to identify three objects with specific characteristics in their surroundings, then listen for distinct sounds, identify several different smells and engage in a simple physical movement, such as stamping their feet," she said. "This rapid redirection of attention helps alleviate immediate physiological stress responses," she said. In addition to patrolling military bases involved in rescue operations on a daily basis, He also goes to the core area to provide on-site assistance when needed. "As members of the military, we cannot shy away from difficult conditions," she said. "I wanted to be on the front line myself — to see if any soldiers needed support and to teach them techniques they can use on their own to manage stress." Tan Xiangdong, Party chief of the Xizang autonomous regional health commission, said at a news conference on Wednesday that national and regional health authorities had organized three batches of psychological health experts, totaling more than 210. Frontline rescuers have access to psychological risk assessments, group and individual counseling, as well as pocket guides designed to help them understand stress reactions and learn effective ways to cope, Tan said. Contact the writers at wangxiaoyu@chinadaily.com.cn For Hao Zhen, who was among a network of volunteers coordinating relief efforts in disaster-hit Gyirong county, rendering aid can come in many forms. When a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong, a remote border area in the Xizang autonomous region, Hao did not hesitate. While professional rescue teams searched the hardest-hit areas, Hao and his fellow volunteers worked behind the scenes to distribute supplies, meals and arrange accommodation for displaced residents and rescue workers. The 27-year-old was among 17 volunteers from China's Go West program who joined relief efforts in Gyirong township after the Aug 26 disaster. "When the disaster first happened, a lot of affected residents and rescuers arrived in the area all at once," Hao said. "The first thing we had to do was make sure they had somewhere to stay and food to eat." As relief supplies poured in, the volunteers counted, sorted and moved thousands of boxes donated by a number of Red Cross organizations, companies and foundations. They also helped with logistics at the local emergency response headquarters and collected and organized information from the disaster area. The experience gave Hao a new understanding of the mechanics of disaster relief efforts. "Before this, I had only read news stories about volunteers helping after disasters," he said. "Now I realize that you don't have to be on the search-and-rescue front line to make a difference. Keeping things running behind the scenes matters, too." Born in 1999, Hao was the oldest among the volunteers working in Gyirong who came from various parts of the country, including Heilongjiang, Jiangxi and Shandong provinces, as well as Xizang, and have backgrounds ranging from medicine to education. The work brought practical challenges. Only two of the 17 volunteers spoke Tibetan, creating communication difficulties at shelters. Local township officials often stepped in to assist with interpretations. Food and accommodation were also stretched in the first few days, as large numbers of residents, rescuers and support workers arrived in the small border town. Hao said the situation gradually improved as local authorities coordinated with hotels and restaurants to provide additional support. Five other Go West program volunteers remained in the county seat, where they welcomed relatives of missing people, assisted families and handled calls and follow-ups through the 12345 public service hotline. Volunteers from nearby counties, including Lhaze and Dingri, also arrived to help. For Hao, Gyirong is a long way from home — nearly 5,700 kilometers from Shuangyashan in Heilongjiang. He usually makes the journey home once a year. He arrived in Gyirong in February 2025 to join the Go West program and planned to stay for three years. His family initially tried to talk him out of the move, worried about the distance and the physical demands of living at high altitude. "But I thought, if everyone worries about the hardship and the distance, places like this will have fewer and fewer young people willing to come," Hao said. The physical challenges are real. When Hao first arrived in Gyirong, he found that he did not have the same stamina he had at lower elevations. He also experienced heart palpitations when he first joined the relief effort. After more than a year on the plateau, however, he said his body has largely adapted. His family still worries about him, particularly after learning that he was involved in the disaster response. "But the disaster happened right here, where we work and live," Hao said. "Since we chose to come here as volunteers, helping when something like this happens is simply part of what we should do." The Aug 26 mudslide at Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. As of 6 pm on Saturday, 43 people had been confirmed dead and 519 others remained missing, according to the local emergency response and rescue command headquarters. For Hao, the experience has also changed the way he approached the small tasks that fill much of his day. Moving boxes, arranging accommodation and making sure people have meals may be far removed from the dramatic scenes of a search-and-rescue operation, but he no longer sees them as minor jobs. "My biggest hope now is that we can keep the support work running smoothly, that all the rescuers return safely and that there are no more secondary disasters," he said. Contact the writers at luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn China has established communication and information-sharing mechanisms with the 23 home countries of the 261 foreign nationals who remain missing following the mudslide that struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border. Through the China-Nepal disaster information exchange mechanism, meteorological, hydrological, glacial lake and glacier data are being transmitted to Nepal daily, a senior official said on Sunday. Ren Wei, executive deputy commander of the emergency rescue headquarters and executive vice-chairman of the Xizang autonomous region, said all relevant information had been promptly communicated to the respective embassies in China through diplomatic channels. A 24-hour dedicated hotline for families of the missing foreign nationals has also been established and has received 509 calls as of Sunday. Each inquiry had been followed up on, with responses relayed to the next of kin, Ren said. At the request of the Nepali side, the Chinese government dispatched tunnel rescue and DNA identification experts to Nepal, along with emergency relief supplies. The Xizang autonomous regional government also provided 320 metric tons of Bailey bridge components — designed for the rapid assembly of temporary bridges — and other relief supplies to Nepal. Yang Lahong, deputy director of the Xizang foreign affairs office, said the region had carried out verification of information on the missing people in a rigorous, prudent and standardized manner. The region released basic information on the missing people initially identified a day after the disaster. On Aug 30, it published additional details of the missing foreign nationals verified through joint investigations and rapid cross-checking by multiple departments. While the breakdown by country and number of missing people was made public by authorities, the specific list and personal details have not been released due to privacy concerns. Instead, the information was communicated to the relevant embassies through diplomatic channels, with a collective briefing held on Tuesday, Yang said. For safety reasons and to ensure efficient and orderly rescue work, no non-professionals were allowed to enter the affected core areas until conditions were fully prepared, she said. To keep the public informed while ensuring safety, a small number of Chinese journalists were arranged to accompany rescue teams into the core areas despite the difficult terrain. Their reports and footage were subsequently released and widely used by domestic and international media, Yang said. Regarding the families of the missing foreign nationals, the region expressed sympathy during these difficult times. In addition to providing regular authoritative updates and notifying families through diplomatic channels, authorities have kept the 24-hour hotline operating, with personnel diligently verifying information and providing feedback. Currently, efforts are focused on rescue and recovery. After the search operation concludes, authorities will confirm and notify the status of deceased foreign nationals and assist their families with follow-up procedures. For those who remain missing, assistance will be provided within China's legal framework, including arrangements for their families to visit Xizang, in coordination with relevant foreign diplomatic missions, she added. Contact the writers at zoushuo@chinadaily.com.cn Chinese experts have intensified monitoring of landslides, barrier lakes, glaciers and glacial lakes around the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong county, Xizang autonomous region, to guard against secondary disasters and ensure the safety of ongoing rescue operations. The mudslide, which occurred on Aug 26, caused significant casualties and left many people missing in the region. Su Pengcheng, a researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said during a group interview with Chinese and foreign media in Gyirong on Sunday that experts from multiple government departments and research institutions had been mobilized soon after the disaster. While rescue operations were underway, specialists began analyzing the causes of the disaster and assessing potential geological risks to provide safety support for frontline rescuers, Su said. The road leading to the core rescue area was reopened in less than a week, while monitoring and risk assessment continued in parallel. One priority has been closely tracking changes in a barrier lake formed after the disaster to prevent any sudden discharge from threatening downstream areas. Authorities have also deployed professional monitoring equipment, including remote slope-deformation cameras, slope radars and satellite remote-sensing systems, to continuously assess the stability of slopes and residual deposits in the disaster-hit area. Particular attention has been paid to potentially unstable material remaining on slopes near the affected valley, which could trigger further landslides or debris flows and pose risks to downstream rescue operations, Su said. Experts have also conducted comprehensive geological hazard surveys around five villages in the affected river basin and along National Highway G216, a key emergency rescue route, to identify potential dangers and ensure the route remains safe. Monitoring has extended beyond the core disaster area, with satellite and aerial remote sensing being used to track changes in surrounding glaciers and glacial lakes, which are widely distributed across the high-altitude region. Su said the operation has brought together expertise from emergency management, natural resources, meteorology and water resources authorities, as well as research institutions, with a range of monitoring equipment deployed. Experts are also using real-time images transmitted by drones to assess changing conditions. Their findings are promptly relayed to downstream teams, allowing search and rescue personnel to adjust operations when risks emerge. Su said the coordinated monitoring system is intended to provide continuous early warning of possible secondary geological disasters while rescue work continues. The recent debris flow that occurred on the Nepali side has underscored the urgent need for cross-border cooperation in disaster early warning, said Norbu Tsering, acting mayor of Shigatse, on Sunday. Su Pengcheng, a researcher at the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, said that source zones of ice-rock avalanches at high altitudes are extremely difficult to access because of cold temperatures, low oxygen levels and rugged terrain. Cross-border river basins also have observational blind spots, while ground equipment can suffer from power and communication problems. Precursor signals are often subtle, and warning windows can be only a matter of minutes — far too short for traditional single-point monitoring to cover entire watersheds, he said. Given that climate change is accelerating such rare but severe events, it is essential to conduct risk assessments of glacier instability, fill upstream monitoring gaps and introduce new geophysical detection technologies for full-chain dynamic monitoring, Su said. He proposed developing a "space-air-ground" noncontact monitoring network to reduce dependence on on-site stations at extreme altitudes. A tiered approach — involving wide-area satellite scanning, targeted high-resolution monitoring and downstream alert systems — could provide valuable additional time for evacuation, he said. Su also called for cross-border scientific collaboration and joint early-warning mechanisms. Since disasters do not respect borders, he called for data exchanges and shared risk assessments with Himalayan nations through existing international platforms. He also urged the creation of rapid notification channels to extend early warnings across entire upstream-downstream basins. Norbu said the Xizang autonomous region has invested heavily in glacial-lake monitoring in recent years. A baseline survey using satellite imagery, fieldwork and glacier data identified more than 33,000 glacial lakes across the region. Authorities have placed 187 high-risk lakes under satellite monitoring, with 49 of those also covered by ground sensors and drone surveillance, he said. A multi-agency data-sharing platform now links meteorological, hydrological, natural resources and emergency departments. Expert panels regularly review glacial-lake risks, and a short-term early-warning system has been activated, along with evacuation drills for downstream communities during the flood season, he said. China has established communication and information-sharing mechanisms with the affected countries as 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries remain missing following a recent mudslide at Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border. Through the China-Nepal disaster information exchange mechanism, meteorological, hydrological, glacial lake, and glacier data are transmitted daily to Nepal, a senior official stated on Sunday. Ren Wei, the executive deputy commander of the emergency rescue headquarters and executive vice-chairman of the Xizang autonomous region, mentioned that all relevant information has been promptly communicated to the respective embassies in China through diplomatic channels. A 24-hour dedicated hotline for families of the missing foreign nationals has been established, receiving 509 calls to date, with each inquiry followed up and responses relayed to the next of kin, Ren added. At Nepal's request, the Chinese government has sent experts in tunnel rescue and DNA identification to Nepal, along with emergency material aid. Additionally, the local government of the Xizang autonomous region has provided 320 metric tons of Bailey bridge components and other relief supplies to Nepal. Yang Lahong, deputy director of the foreign affairs office of the Xizang autonomous region, noted that the region has rigorously and prudently verified the personnel information of the missing individuals. The basic information of the missing persons was initially released the day after the disaster, and further details were published on Aug 30, verified through joint investigations and rapid cross-checking by multiple departments. While the breakdown by country and number has been made public, specific lists and personal details have not been released due to privacy concerns; instead, this information has been communicated to the relevant embassies through diplomatic channels, with a collective briefing held on Sept 1, she said. For safety reasons and to ensure efficient and orderly rescue work, non-professionals were not allowed into the affected core areas until conditions were fully prepared. To keep the public informed while ensuring safety, a small number of Chinese journalists accompanied rescue teams into the core areas, overcoming difficult terrain. Their reports and footage were subsequently released and widely used by domestic and international media, Yang said. Regarding the families of the missing foreign nationals, the region expressed empathy, offering full understanding and care. In addition to regular authoritative updates and diplomatic notifications, a 24-hour hotline was set up and has received hundreds of calls, with staff diligently verifying and feeding back information. Currently, efforts are focused on rescue and recovery. After the search operation concludes, authorities will confirm and notify the status of deceased foreign nationals and assist families with follow-up procedures. For those still missing, assistance will be provided within China's legal framework, including arrangements for families visiting Xizang, in coordination with relevant foreign diplomatic missions, she added. Visiting the mudslide-hit area at Gyirong Port in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region on Sunday, two foreign journalists were impressed by China's response to the disaster and urged the international community to work together in tackling climate change. Reporters: Wang Xiaoyu, Palden Nyima and Shu Yiheng Video editor: Song Yi Editor: Liu Ming GYIRONG, Xizang -- China has provided assistance to 1,720 Nepalese border residents after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region on Aug 26, the emergency response and rescue headquarters said on Sunday. The mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, had left 43 people dead and 519 others missing at the border port as of 6 pm Saturday, officials told a news conference. Many Nepalese border residents who work or do business in the county of Gyirong were stranded there after the mudslide destroyed the border port, through which they enter and leave China. After a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong Port in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region on Aug 26, 27-year-old Hao Zhen and 16 other volunteers from the "Go West" program joined the relief effort. Working behind the scenes in Gyirong town, the volunteers arranged accommodation, distributed supplies and helped provide meals for displaced residents and rescue workers. Hao said his comrades and himself were committed to playing their part wherever the motherland and the people needed them. GYIRONG, Xizang -- China has deployed more than 2,500 rescue personnel after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region on Aug 26, the emergency response and rescue headquarters said on Sunday. As of 6 pm Saturday, more than 2,500 people and over 500 vehicles had been deployed to join rescue operations, and more than 1,000 flights of drones had air-dropped 5.43 metric tons of supplies, officials said. GYIRONG, Xizang -- Forty-three people had been confirmed dead and 519 others remained missing as of 6 pm Saturday after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region on Aug 26, local emergency response and rescue authorities said on Sunday. A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as being among the missing, officials told a press conference attended by domestic and foreign journalists. The press conference was held after journalists from overseas media outlets visited the mudslide site at Gyirong Port over the weekend. China launched a massive search and rescue operation after the deadly mudslide, which was triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal. As of 6 pm Saturday, China has deployed more than 2,500 people and over 500 vehicles to join rescue operations. Drones have conducted more than 1,000 flights, and 5.43 tonnes of supplies have been air-dropped. Local authorities have provided assistance to 1,720 Nepalese border residents in Gyirong. Many Nepalese nationals who work or do business in Gyirong were stranded there after the mudslide destroyed the border port, through which they normally enter and leave China. China has also provided Nepal with daily updates on meteorological, hydrological and glacier data through a disaster information notification mechanism, according to officials. Until last month, Hao Zhen had only seen disaster relief efforts on the news. Then a devastating mudslide struck Gyirong, the remote border county in Xizang autonomous region where he works as a volunteer. While professional rescue teams searched the hardest-hit areas, Hao and his fellow volunteers worked behind the scenes, arranging accommodation, distributing supplies and helping provide meals for displaced residents and rescue workers. "When the disaster first happened, a lot of affected residents and rescuers arrived in the township all at once," Hao said. As relief supplies poured in, the volunteers counted, sorted and moved thousands of boxes donated by Red Cross organizations, companies and foundations. They also helped with logistical work at the local emergency response headquarters and collected and organized information from the disaster area. The experience gave Hao a new understanding of what disaster relief involves. Born in 1999, Hao is the oldest of the 17 Go West program volunteers working in Gyirong township. Most of the others were born between 2000 and 2003. They come from across China, including Heilongjiang, Jiangxi and Shandong provinces, as well as Xizang, and have backgrounds ranging from medicine to education. The work has come with practical challenges. Only two of the 17 volunteers speak Tibetan, creating communication difficulties at the shelters. Local township officials often stepped in to interpret. Food and accommodation were also stretched in the first few days as large numbers of residents, rescuers and support workers arrived in the small border town. Hao said the situation gradually improved as local authorities coordinated with hotels and restaurants to provide additional support. Another five Go West program volunteers remained in the county seat, helping receive relatives of missing people, assisting families and handling calls and follow-ups through the 12345 public service hotline. Volunteers from nearby counties, including Lhaze and Dingri, also came to help. For Hao, Gyirong is a long way from home — nearly 5,700 kilometers from Shuangyashan in Heilongjiang province. He usually makes the journey home only once a year. He arrived in Gyirong in February 2025 to join the Go West program and plans to stay for three years. His family initially tried to talk him out of the move, worried about the distance and the physical demands of living at high altitude. The physical challenges are real. When Hao first arrived in Gyirong, he found he did not have the same stamina he had at lower elevations. He also experienced heart palpitations when he first joined the relief effort. After more than a year on the plateau, however, he said his body has largely adapted. The Aug 26 mudslide at Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. As of Friday evening, 31 people had been confirmed dead and 531 remained missing in Gyirong, according to the local emergency response and rescue command headquarters. For Hao, the experience has also changed the way he sees the small tasks that fill much of his day. KATHMANDU -- Nepali rescuers on Saturday rescued a Chinese national from a hydropower plant hit by the deadly mudslide in Nepal, according to the Chinese Embassy in Nepal. The Chinese national was rescued by the Nepali Army in coordination with a disaster expert team from South Korea, 11 days after a devastating mudslide struck the area. The survivor was taken for further medical assessment and care. The rescue is part of an intensified effort to locate and evacuate people believed to be trapped inside hydropower project tunnels following a mudslide that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems. The disaster caused extensive damage to several hydropower projects and other infrastructure in the affected areas. Some workers and other people are believed to have been trapped inside hydropower tunnels and have remained out of contact. Before the rescue of the Chinese national, the Nepali Army said in a social media post that a joint rescue team comprising 20 Nepali Army personnel and project representatives had been conducting search operations. The Nepali Army has been conducting search and rescue operations in coordination with foreign technical teams, including experts from China, India and South Korea, to reach people stranded inside structures at several hydropower projects. China has deployed around 20 sets of monitoring equipment across the disaster-hit Gyirong area in the Xizang autonomous region, with real-time data showing geological conditions stabilizing, a senior geologist said. The devices — including debris flow monitors, slope radars and microseismic sensors — were installed by the China Geological Survey and other emergency response teams following last month's ice-rock avalanche that buried parts of the Gyirong border crossing, causing massive casualties on both sides of the border. Ge Daqing, deputy director of the China Aero Geophysical Survey and Remote Sensing Center for Natural Resources, said the equipment was positioned at key risk points across the disaster zone to monitor slope movement, debris flow channels and ground deformation in real time. Two additional slope radars were installed on Wednesday near the border crossing after rescue teams cleared access roads, he added. The devices are positioned to protect workers repairing roads and power lines by issuing early warnings if falling rocks or shallow landslides are detected on the slopes above. Data collected so far indicates the dynamic processes at the site have entered a relatively stable phase. "Overall, there have been no significant fluctuations or changes," Ge said, adding that the risk of a large-scale secondary disaster is currently assessed as low without external triggers. However, he cautioned that high-risk factors persist due to the complex terrain. Some minor rockfalls have been observed at the glacier front in the collapse zone, but Ge said these pose no immediate threat. The monitoring equipment is primarily intended for the emergency response phase. Once a comprehensive risk assessment is completed and no major threats remain, the devices may be withdrawn, he said. Beyond the immediate response, the disaster has underscored the limitations of existing monitoring technologies in the high-altitude, cloud-prone Himalayan region. Ge said optical satellite imagery — the most common remote sensing tool — is severely hampered by persistent cloud cover and fog in the area. Clear images can be obtained on only about 20 days a year, and most of the optical data received recently have been obscured by clouds. To address this, Ge called for the accelerated development of new synthetic aperture radar satellites, particularly an interferometric SAR satellite constellation that combines L-band, high-resolution, wide-swath capabilities, and both sun-synchronous and low-inclination orbits. This can overcome the challenge of monitoring rapid deformation in the high-elevation mountains and glaciers of the Himalayas. He also stressed the need to improve satellite revisit cycles and spatial resolution to enable more frequent and rapid monitoring. Unmanned aerial vehicles offer another monitoring option, but current drones struggle to operate above 7,000 meters and their sensors remain vulnerable to cloud interference. New radar-based sensors and improved high-altitude flight capabilities are needed, he added. Looking ahead, Ge warned that the risk of high-altitude ice-rock avalanches in the region is likely to increase. "The 2015 Nepal earthquake caused internal damage to these mountain masses," he said. "Combined with glacial erosion at high elevations and steep terrain, the structural integrity of rock formations has been compromised, making them prone to collapse." Given the transboundary nature of such hazards, Ge highlighted the importance of international collaboration in disaster monitoring and early warning across the Himalayan region, noting that ice-rock avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods do not respect national borders. limenghan@chinadaily.com.cn The death toll from the massive mudslide that struck a border port in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, on Aug 26, rose to 31 as of 6 pm on Friday, while 531 people remained missing. A total of 987 personal items had also been recovered, according to the disaster emergency and rescue command headquarters. The rescue access route to Gyirong Port has been opened, marking a new stage in relief efforts, the headquarters said at a news conference on Friday evening. The command center said coordinated rescue operations would be further intensified, with particular emphasis on monitoring and early warning for secondary disasters at the port site and along the G216 highway. Local authorities will also continue to assess risks and issue early warnings for areas upstream and downstream of the disaster site to ensure the safety of rescue operations, the headquarters said. Since the mudslide hit Gyirong Port, an important land gateway between China and Nepal, round-the-clock rescue operations involving multiple government departments have been underway. As of 4 pm on Wednesday, 172 experts and technicians from meteorological, natural resources, water resources and emergency management departments, along with 150 sets of equipment, had been deployed to the site, according to the headquarters. The water resources authority, for example, sent 28 experts with 31 sets of equipment, including drones, radar water-level gauges and high-definition cameras, to conduct hydrological monitoring. The natural resources department dispatched 92 technicians with 40 sets of equipment to carry out focused surveys along two rescue access routes and in areas affected by the mudslide. The regional government has also moved swiftly to assess geological hazards in the disaster area. As of Wednesday, a special inspection along the G216 highway, a key rescue access route, had identified 58 geological hazard sites. Seven were classified as high-risk, 39 as medium-risk and 12 as low-risk, according to the headquarters. Local authorities have completed hazard inspections and risk assessments in three affected villages and identified two sites for temporary shelters, while providing guidance on their construction, the headquarters said. Technology has played a key role in the rescue operation. Slope radar, high-definition video surveillance and geophone monitoring systems have been installed in areas affected by ice-avalanche debris flows to continuously detect anomalies, including ice-rock collapses and deformation of debris in the source zone. By automatically collecting deformation and image data, the systems help address the limitations of manual inspections in the steep, canyon-locked terrain. They enable real-time monitoring of key hazard sites and help ensure the safety of rescue personnel working downstream, the command center said. In addition, local authorities have established a regular coordination mechanism to ensure smooth information flow throughout the rescue operation. Medical and epidemic prevention personnel from the Chinese military have begun testing soil samples from the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in Shigatse, Xizang autonomous region, to help formulate disinfection and personal protection plans as detailed search and rescue efforts continue. Bacterial culture and pathogen testing are being used to gauge the risk of infectious diseases for rescue crews working amid shattered rocks and thick sludge in the core area, said a medical and disease prevention team with the People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command's logistics support department. The road access was largely restored on Wednesday morning. Lhamo Tsering, a military technician specializing in infectious disease prevention and control, said that soil samples collected from the core zone would go through testing for 21 vector-borne pathogens, 23 respiratory pathogens and 32 gastrointestinal pathogens. "Conducting pathogen testing on these soil samples can identify the types and levels of soil pathogen contamination, assess the risk of secondary infectious diseases, trace the sources of pollution, and guide environmental disinfection and personnel protection," she said. "The results can also help us evaluate the effectiveness of epidemic control efforts and prevent the spread of soil-borne infectious diseases after a disaster," she added. Liu Xiaonan, a member of the team, was among the first to enter the core zone on Wednesday after the road leading to the port reopened. He recalled heavy downpours that evening, and his team worked until late before returning. One of the most challenging parts of his work was navigating the deep mud in the area. "In some areas, the sludge looks solid, but when I try walking on it, my feet can get sucked down until the mud comes up to my calves or even my knees. Sometimes we are only able to pull ourselves out with the help of nearby personnel," he said. It is also important to prevent mosquito and other insect bites in the area, he added. Lhamo Tsering was one of the two female military personnel working on-site on Friday morning. The other was tasked with providing psychological consulting for search and rescue crew members. Lhamo Tsering said she had participated in responding to acute health emergencies, including the COVID-19 outbreak, in the past. It was her first time working on the front line in the aftermath of a devastating natural disaster of this scale. "I am used to performing tests in the laboratory using samples collected and transported back by my fellow soldiers. This time, I asked to come to the hardest-hit area because I wanted to collect the samples myself to ensure the precision of my work," she said. As a native of Lhasa, the regional capital of Xizang, Lhamo Tsering said she was also deeply saddened by the havoc wreaked by the mudslide at Gyirong Port. "This area is naturally beautiful with pristine air, a comfortable altitude and lush vegetation," she said. "I hope that one day it can restore its beauty." Despite his weary appearance, he insisted repeatedly that he was not tired at all. "All I want is to find my workmates," he said on Thursday, gripping an iron shovel with determination, his brow furrowed. On Aug 26, a massive mudslide devastated Gyirong Port, a vital land link between China and Nepal. By Wednesday noon, 21 victims had been found, 847 personal belongings recovered, and 541 people remained missing. Xiao was driving toward the port when the disaster struck. "I was just four or five kilometers away when I saw several cars pulled over," he said. "I got out and asked other drivers what was happening — everyone was panicked, saying the water level had risen sharply near the port." Concerned for their safety, he instructed the two female colleagues in his car to get out and find a safe place, then continued driving alone to assess the situation. Upon realizing it was a landslide, Xiao immediately alerted the authorities. "The muddy water was rushing toward me, so I threw the car into reverse and backed up about 500 meters before stopping," he recounted, his voice tense. "I was terrified the car would be swept away. What really scared me was not knowing what had happened to my workmates at the port." Originally from Qinghai province, the 39-year-old Xiao has worked in Xizang for 17 years, with 11 of those years at the Gyirong entry-exit border inspection station, primarily handling publicity affairs. "For many years, I've spent almost every day with my workmates — filming their patrols, writing about their lives guarding this border," he said. "This port, these people — they've become part of me." On the first day of the rescue, Xiao and other workers camped in a tent by a reservoir halfway up the mountain near the border port. He did not sleep at all. "The rain was so heavy that night — water poured down the slopes and merged into the river. The sound of rain, rushing water, and collapsing hillsides all mixed together. It made my heart sink. I didn't dare to sleep, and I couldn't sleep anyway," he said.

item.title: Services emerging as key driver for trade growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-07
Services emerging as key driver for trade growth Knowledge-intensive exports lead structural upgrade as CIFTIS promotes 2-way opening amid protectionism headwinds China's trade in services saw rapid expansion in the first half, officials, experts and business executives said, pointing to a shift toward a foreign trade structure in which services are an increasingly important source of growth. Buoyed by the sector's robust expansion, the China International Fair for Trade in Services is set to further cement its role as a two-way gateway, accelerating the flow of global innovation into China's vast market while helping Chinese service providers make further inroads in markets overseas. Opening in Beijing on Wednesday, the five-day fair is expected to draw growing international attention, underscoring China's commitment to opening its services sector wider and injecting much-needed stability and certainty into global trade amid mounting protectionism and heightened economic uncertainty, they added. In contrast to goods trade, which involves physical products moving across borders, services trade covers transactions in intangible offerings ranging from transportation and tourism to telecommunications, advertising, education, computing and accounting. In the first half, China's imports and exports of services totaled 3.78 trillion yuan ($556.6 billion), up 8.3 percent year-on-year, said the Ministry of Commerce. That was nearly 50 percent higher than in the same period a decade earlier, when the total stood at 2.53 trillion yuan. Growth has gathered pace in recent years, with annual two-way services trade topping $1 trillion for the first time in 2024, the ministry said. "China's services trade is expanding rapidly and becoming more competitive. It has emerged as a particularly resilient source of growth in the country's opening-up drive," said Wang Peng, a researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences. That growing strength is drawing businesses from around the world, with a strong international presence expected at the event. "This year's fair will bring together some 90 countries and international organizations, with more than 1,800 companies set to exhibit on-site," Vice-Minister of Commerce Yan Dong said at a recent news conference in Beijing. Falkor, a Norway-based industrial intelligence provider serving the global energy sector, will make its fifth appearance at CIFTIS this year, showcasing its solutions, real-world applications and the results of its work with industry partners, said Wu Haifeng, senior vice-president of Falkor. Norway will serve as the guest country of honor at this year's fair. Wu, who is also vice-chairman of the Norwegian Business Association China, said Norwegian businesses hope to use the occasion to forge new partnerships in China. At last year's fair, the company formed a strategic partnership with China Oil HBP Science & Technology Co. The two sides have since been working to roll out an industrial digital platform, Wu said. "Over the next five years, we will continue to increase our investment in China, deepen local partnerships, and use industrial intelligence to boost operational performance and advance the energy sector's green transition," Wu said. Meanwhile, this year's fair will see more than 90 companies and institutions unveil new technologies, products and services spanning information and communications technology, fintech and digital healthcare, with some set for global debuts or their first showings in China, Yan added. Johnson & Johnson MedTech, the medical technology arm of US healthcare giant Johnson & Johnson, will bring more than 60 products to the fair. About one-third will make their CIFTIS debut, said Edward Zhou, president of Johnson& Johnson MedTech China. "We have been part of CIFTIS for several years now, and what sets this platform apart is its ability to turn conversations into action. It is more than a showcase — it is a catalyst," Zhou said. Impella, a minimally invasive heart pump featured at last year's fair, has since secured temporary import approval under a program for innovative medical devices needed in clinical care and entered clinical use at leading cardiac centers in Beijing, he said, adding that "what we see in China's services trade is a clear shift toward quality-driven growth".
